speaker: Tobias Lütke
title: Tobi Lütke: 21 Years of Building Shopify
question: At a public technology company, why do traditional multi-year stock option grants fail employees after a steep stock drop?
guest: People got stock options at the peak level, and I realized the psychological problem with everyone being so underwater and having to spend years getting back to the zero point where the stock options are worth even a penny again. And of course they felt the company gave them those things at the time—they were passive in this interaction, therefore the company has some kind of responsibility to make them whole. Even though other people voting in the market caused the price, I received the point that they had no agency in the process. So we rebuilt our compensation system to work the opposite way: you get your annual number and sliders to decide every quarter how much you want in cash, RSUs, or stock options. The consequence is beautiful—if the stock goes down, you now get more stock options in your next quarter, so it rebalances against actual value every quarter, and you have full agency over the choice.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Traditional multi-year option grants fail after a steep stock drop because their value depends entirely on the share price rising above a strike price that was fixed on the grant date. When the stock falls well below that strike, the options go "underwater": exercising them would mean paying more than the shares are worth, so they have no intrinsic value, even though the employee is still vesting into them for years.

The multi-year structure makes this worse. A large upfront grant locks in one strike price for the whole four-year period, so a single badly timed grant date can wipe out most of an employee's expected equity compensation, with no automatic reset. Unlike RSUs, which keep some value at any share price, options can lose all of it.

The consequences follow directly. The grant stops working as a retention or incentive tool, since employees can leave and get fresh equity priced at current market levels elsewhere, or see newer hires receive lower strikes for the same job. Companies then face awkward fixes, such as repricing, option exchanges, or supplemental grants, which cost money, dilute shareholders, and often require shareholder approval.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Traditional multi-year stock option grants lock in a fixed strike price equal to the company’s share price on a single grant date. When a public tech company’s stock plunges, that strike price ends up far above the current market value, rendering the options "underwater" and intrinsically worthless. Unlike restricted stock units (RSUs), which retain reduced value as long as the stock stays above zero, options pay nothing unless shares rebound past their original grant price—a recovery that can take years or never materialize. Because a multi-year grant is meant to deliver compensation over roughly four years, a steep drop effectively erases a large portion of an employee's ongoing pay. Worse, it creates sharp internal inequity: new hires receive grants priced at the depressed market value with far greater upside, while tenured employees vest into worthless options for the same work. Unless the company undertakes a costly option repricing or issues extra refresh grants, the retention incentive vanishes, prompting experienced employees to leave for competitors offering fresh equity at current valuations.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Traditional option grants fail employees after a steep drop because the strike price is locked at the grant-date share price, often near a peak, while the shares vest over four years. If the stock then falls sharply, the options go "underwater." Their exercise price is above market value, so they're worth nothing unless the stock recovers past that old level. Employees keep vesting into paper with no value, and the pay they counted on disappears.

That breaks the grant's purpose. The "golden handcuffs" stop holding anyone, since there's nothing to lose by leaving, and new hires granted at the lower price can end up better off than long-tenured colleagues. That breeds resentment and pushes people to leave. Fixing it is hard for a public company. Repricing or exchanging options usually needs shareholder approval, draws criticism from proxy advisors, and adds accounting cost and dilution.

So the grant's value depends on the share price on one date rather than on the employee's ongoing work. That's why many tech companies have moved to RSUs, which keep some value after a drop, and to shorter, annual or one-year grants.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Traditional multi-year stock option grants typically lock in a fixed exercise price equal to the company’s stock price on the grant date, vesting over several years. After a steep stock drop, those options go "underwater"—meaning the market price falls below the exercise price—leaving them with zero immediate value. Even as employees continue vesting new options each month, they receive no financial benefit unless the stock recovers all the way back above the original grant price, which can take years or never happen.

This breaks both compensation and retention. Because equity makes up a large share of total pay at public tech companies, underwater options amount to a steep, prolonged pay cut. Worse, newly hired peers receive grants priced at the much lower current share price and profit immediately from any partial rebound, creating sharp internal pay disparities. Faced with years of waiting just to break even while competitors offer fresh, lower-priced equity, tenured employees often conclude that leaving makes more financial sense than staying.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol

Traditional stock options give employees the right to buy shares at a price fixed when the grant is issued. After a steep stock drop, that exercise price can sit far above the market price. The options are then underwater. Even as more options vest, employees get no financial benefit from exercising them unless the stock climbs above the original exercise price before the options expire.

That means the stock can recover substantially and employees can spend years earning the rest of their grant without realizing any value from it. Meanwhile, new hires may receive options with lower exercise prices and benefit from the same recovery. The old grants lose much of their power to retain employees precisely when the company needs them to stay.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A traditional stock option gives an employee the right to buy shares at a price fixed when the grant is made. If the stock falls below that price, the option is “underwater.” Even after it vests, exercising it would cost more than buying the same shares on the market. For example, if an option has a $100 exercise price and the stock falls to $40, the stock can double to $80 and the employee still earns no gain from exercising it.

The option can regain value if the stock recovers before it expires. But because the exercise price stays fixed across years of vesting, one steep drop can leave several years of expected compensation with little motivational or retention value.
